questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is evaluated for chronic watery diarrhea, failure to thrive, and weeping eczematous skin lesions. Laboratory studies show hyperglycemia consistent with new-onset type 1 diabetes and a markedly elevated serum IgE. A maternal uncle died in infancy of similar problems. Genetic testing identifies a loss-of-function mutation. Deficiency of which of the following is most directly responsible for this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B-cell receptor editing in the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fas-mediated apoptosis of lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class II expression on thymic epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymic negative selection of CD8+ T cells

explanation.summary: Loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3 abolish functional regulatory T cells, producing IPEX syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that X-linked loss-of-function mutations in the FOXP3 gene cause IPEX (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked). Because FOXP3 is the master transcription factor for regulatory T cells, patients cannot generate functional Tregs and develop multi-organ autoimmunity (enteropathy, endocrinopathy such as type 1 diabetes) plus allergic inflammation in early infancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor editing is a B-cell central tolerance mechanism in the bone marrow and is unrelated to this Treg-deficiency syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective Fas-mediated apoptosis causes ALPS, which presents with lymphoproliferation (splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy) and autoimmune cytopenias, not this autoimmune enteropathy/diabetes/eczema picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Absent MHC class II (bare lymphocyte syndrome) causes an immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, not this triad of autoimmunity and allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The enteropathy-endocrinopathy-eczema triad with elevated IgE in an X-linked infant is the FOXP3/Treg phenotype of IPEX; thymic negative selection is not the specifically implicated process here.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: During T-cell development, a thymocyte in the thymic medulla expresses a T-cell receptor that binds a self-peptide-MHC complex on a thymic epithelial cell with very high affinity. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anergy induced by lack of costimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apoptosis through negative selection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Differentiation into a CD8+ cytotoxic effector cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive selection and export to the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing of its antigen receptor

explanation.summary: Thymocytes that bind self-peptide-MHC with high affinity are deleted by negative selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in the thymic medulla, developing single-positive T cells undergo negative selection: if they bind self-peptide-MHC with too strong an affinity, they are eliminated by apoptosis. This prevents strongly self-reactive T cells from reaching the periphery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is a peripheral tolerance mechanism resulting from lack of costimulation, not the fate of a thymocyte during central selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Strong self-binders are eliminated, not permitted to mature into effector cells; only intermediate binders may become Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cells that bind self-peptide-MHC only weakly are the ones positively selected and released to the circulation; strong binders are deleted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a B-cell process in the bone marrow; T cells do not edit their receptors.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has had years of massive nontender lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly along with recurrent autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Peripheral blood shows an expanded population of autoreactive lymphocytes. A defect in which of the following best explains her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD28-B7 costimulation of T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fas-FasL-mediated apoptosis of lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Generation of regulatory T cells in the thymus

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgA secretion across the gut epithelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive selection in the thymic cortex

explanation.summary: Defective Fas-induced apoptosis causes autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that individuals with defects in Fas-induced apoptosis accumulate circulating autoreactive T cells, producing ALPS. It presents in childhood with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy from lymphocyte buildup, and patients are susceptible to autoimmune cytopenias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CD28-B7 costimulation defect would impair T-cell activation, not cause lymphocyte accumulation and autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of Treg generation causes IPEX, which presents in infancy with autoimmune enteropathy and endocrinopathy, not this chronic lymphoproliferation with cytopenias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gut IgA secretion relates to oral tolerance and has no role in this systemic lymphoproliferative, cytopenic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive-selection defect would reduce the number of mature T cells (immunodeficiency), not cause accumulation of autoreactive lymphocytes.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In an experiment, a naive CD4+ T cell encounters its cognate peptide-MHC complex on a resting antigen-presenting cell that does not express B7. The T cell survives but becomes unable to respond even when later given a fully activating stimulus. This state is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anergy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clonal expansion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative selection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive selection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing

explanation.summary: Recognition of antigen without CD28-B7 costimulation induces T-cell anergy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that priming requires TCR binding to peptide-MHC plus costimulation through CD28-B7. When a T cell recognizes antigen without the CD28-B7 signal, it becomes anergic, a state of non-responsiveness that also shortens the cell's lifespan. B7 is upregulated on activated APCs, so T cells are normally primed only in an inflammatory environment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonal expansion is the outcome of successful activation, the opposite of the non-responsive state described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection is deletion of self-reactive thymocytes in the thymus, not a peripheral response to missing costimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive selection occurs in the thymic cortex during development and does not describe this peripheral event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow B-cell mechanism and does not apply to a peripheral T cell.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic melanoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody directed against CTLA-4 and subsequently develops immune-mediated colitis and hypophysitis. Under normal conditions, CTLA-4 maintains peripheral tolerance by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding PD-L1 to deliver an inhibitory signal to T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competing with CD28 for B7, reducing T-cell costimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delivering perforin and granzymes into autoreactive T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Editing the T-cell receptor to remove self-reactivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestering IL-2 through a high-affinity receptor

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 dampens T-cell activation by outcompeting CD28 for B7.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that CTLA-4 molecules on Treg cells compete with CD28 for the binding of B7. When CTLA-4 binds B7 instead of CD28, the amount of B7 available to costimulate T cells through CD28 is reduced, suppressing activation. Blocking CTLA-4 therapeutically removes this brake and can trigger autoimmune toxicities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding PD-L1 to shut off the activation signal is the mechanism of PD-1, a different checkpoint receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Killing autoreactive T cells with perforin and granzymes is a separate Treg suppressive mechanism, not how CTLA-4 works.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T cells do not undergo receptor editing; that mechanism is limited to developing B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequestering IL-2 is accomplished by the high-affinity IL-2 receptor CD25, a distinct Treg mechanism.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A solid tumor biopsy shows abundant tumor-cell expression of PD-L1 and heavy infiltration by regulatory T cells, with poorly functioning cytotoxic T cells. Tumor PD-L1 most directly suppresses the T-cell response by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking B7 from binding CD28 on T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Engaging PD-1 to switch off the T-cell activation signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inducing receptor editing in tumor-infiltrating B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preventing positive selection of thymocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secreting IL-10 and TGF-beta from the tumor cells

explanation.summary: Tumor PD-L1 engages PD-1 on T cells to turn off their activation signal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that PD-1 on T cells turns off the activation signal when it encounters its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, and that tumors exploit this by expressing PD-L1 to escape immune death. Stable tumors are also often infiltrated by regulatory T cells, consistent with the biopsy findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Competing with CD28 for B7 is the mechanism of CTLA-4, not of PD-L1 engaging PD-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow B-cell central tolerance process, not a function of tumor PD-L1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive selection occurs in the thymus and is irrelevant to a peripheral tumor microenvironment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although tumors do express anti-inflammatory molecules, PD-L1 is a surface ligand that acts by engaging PD-1, not by secreting cytokines.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: An immature B cell in the bone marrow binds a self-antigen through its B-cell receptor. Rather than dying, it initiates a new round of V-J recombination at a light-chain locus, replacing its light chain and producing a receptor that no longer binds self-antigen. This rescue process is called which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affinity maturation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class-switch recombination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative selection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor editing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic hypermutation

explanation.summary: Salvaging a self-reactive B cell by new light-chain rearrangement is receptor editing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that some self-reactive immature B cells are salvaged rather than deleted: through receptor editing the cell starts another round of V-J recombination at the kappa or lambda light-chain loci to generate a receptor that no longer binds self-antigen, allowing it to leave the bone marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity maturation is the germinal-center process that increases receptor affinity, unrelated to this bone-marrow rescue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain isotype of the antibody, not the light chain used for tolerance editing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection deletes the self-reactive cell by apoptosis; here the cell is instead rescued.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation occurs in germinal centers to increase antibody affinity, not to remove self-reactivity during central tolerance.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Regulatory T cells constitutively express CD25, the high-affinity alpha-chain of the IL-2 receptor. This feature contributes to peripheral tolerance primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consuming local IL-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Editing the antigen receptors of neighboring T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presenting self-antigen on MHC class II to delete effector T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Providing costimulation to autoreactive T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secreting perforin to lyse dendritic cells

explanation.summary: The high-affinity IL-2 receptor lets Tregs soak up IL-2 needed by other T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists expression of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor (CD25) as a Treg suppressive mechanism: the receptor soaks up available IL-2, an important T-cell proliferation and survival factor, so that with less IL-2 other T cells are deprived.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor editing occurs only in developing B cells and cannot be performed on neighboring T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tregs suppress responses rather than presenting self-antigen to actively delete effector T cells; that is not the role of CD25.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tregs inhibit costimulation (for example via CTLA-4); they do not provide costimulation to autoreactive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tregs can kill autoreactive T cells with perforin and granzymes, but that is a separate mechanism distinct from the IL-2 sequestration function of CD25.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with a severe peanut allergy (anaphylaxis to trace amounts) completes a year of oral immunotherapy and can now eat a few peanuts without reaction. Her response has shifted from a Th2/IgE-dominated one toward one dominated by regulatory T cells and IgA. This tolerance was most likely established by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fas-mediated deletion of all peanut-reactive B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: FcgammaRIIB-mediated shutdown of mast cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of CD40-CD40L costimulation in the draining lymph node

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negative selection of peanut-reactive thymocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tolerogenic gut dendritic cells inducing regulatory T cells

explanation.summary: Oral tolerance is driven by tolerogenic gut dendritic cells that generate induced Tregs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that in the gut, tolerogenic dendritic cells promote differentiation of T cells into regulatory T cells (induced Tregs) via retinoic acid and TGF-beta, generating anti-inflammatory responses to food antigens. This matches the case where slow oral exposure shifted the peanut response from Th2/IgE toward Tregs and IgA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The described Treg/IgA shift reflects active regulation, not wholesale Fas-mediated deletion of peanut-reactive B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FcgammaRIIB is a B-cell inhibitory receptor and is not the driver of this Th2-to-Treg shift.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of CD40 help causes B-cell anergy generally, but it is not the gut mechanism that generates induced Tregs during oral tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Central tolerance in the thymus cannot select against a food antigen encountered later in life; oral tolerance is a peripheral mechanism.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: During a normal pregnancy the maternal immune system does not reject the fetus, whose tissues express antigens from the other biological parent. Which of the following best explains this immune privilege at the maternal-fetal interface?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maternal and fetal blood mix freely, diluting reactive lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal B cells undergo receptor editing against paternal antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placental cells express Fas ligand and suppress local lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fetal thymus negatively selects maternal T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fetus lacks all MHC molecules and is therefore immunologically invisible

explanation.summary: The placenta actively enforces immune privilege through FasL, Tregs, and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that Tregs help prevent an immune response against fetal tissues, that TGF-beta and IL-10 are increased at the placental barrier, and that placental cells express Fas ligand to induce apoptosis in lymphocytes that cross the barrier. Immune privilege is thus actively generated, not merely a physical barrier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick specifically notes the two blood supplies do not directly mix, so dilution by mixing is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow central tolerance process and is not the mechanism of maternal-fetal immune privilege.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fetal thymus selects the fetus's own developing T cells; it does not negatively select maternal T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick states privilege is actively generated; the fetus is not simply MHC-null and invisible.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A self-reactive B cell in a lymph node binds a T-dependent self-antigen with its B-cell receptor but receives no CD40-mediated help from a helper T cell, because the corresponding self-reactive helper T cells have already been tolerized. Which of the following is the most likely outcome for this B cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes anergic and non-responsive

choices.label: B
choices.text: It differentiates into a regulatory B cell in the thymus

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is positively selected and enters the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It performs receptor editing to change its heavy chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: It undergoes robust clonal expansion and antibody secretion

explanation.summary: A self-reactive B cell that gets no T-cell (CD40) help becomes anergic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that B cells require a second signal (CD40) to respond to T-dependent antigens; if a B cell recognizes a self-peptide and does not receive help from T cells, it becomes anergic. Because the helper T cells needed to provide CD40 signaling are already tolerized, the B cell cannot be activated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B cells do not mature in the thymus, and differentiation into a thymic regulatory B cell is not a described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Positive selection is a bone-marrow central tolerance event, not a peripheral response to lack of T-cell help.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor editing occurs in the bone marrow and involves the light chain, not peripheral heavy-chain editing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Without the required second signal, the B cell cannot be fully activated to expand and secrete antibody.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In the periphery, high levels of circulating IgG engage a low-affinity inhibitory Fc receptor on B cells, downregulating antibody production and promoting apoptosis. Which of the following receptors mediates this inhibitory signal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD28

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD40

choices.label: C
choices.text: CTLA-4

choices.label: D
choices.text: FcgammaRIIB

choices.label: E
choices.text: PD-1

explanation.summary: FcgammaRIIB is the inhibitory IgG Fc receptor that dampens B-cell responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that B cells express inhibitory receptors, the most studied being FcgammaRIIB, a low-affinity receptor for IgG. When IgG levels are high and sufficient FcgammaRIIB binding occurs, the resulting signals downregulate antibody production, prevent signaling through the BCR, and promote apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 is a costimulatory, activating receptor on T cells, not a B-cell inhibitory Fc receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD40 delivers activating help (signal 2) to B cells rather than an inhibitory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CTLA-4 is expressed on T cells and inhibits by competing for B7; it is not an Fc receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-1 is an inhibitory checkpoint receptor on T cells, not the B-cell receptor for IgG Fc.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A tissue macrophage in a healthy, uninfected joint is continuously exposed to normal self-proteins released during routine cell turnover, yet it does not become activated or initiate inflammation. Which of the following best explains why the innate immune system does not need a dedicated tolerance-screening process to avoid attacking self?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It requires CD28-B7 costimulation before it can respond to any stimulus

choices.label: B
choices.text: It undergoes receptor editing after binding a self-protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its pattern recognition receptors bind only pathogen- and damage-associated patterns

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its receptors are deleted in the thymus if they bind self-antigen too strongly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory T cells continuously sequester the IL-2 it needs to activate

explanation.summary: Innate cells avoid self by design: PRRs recognize only PAMPs and DAMPs, so without pathogens or damage they stay quiet.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the innate immune system limits its defense to foreign invaders through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which recognize only pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns. Without pathogens or damage, the innate immune system does not activate. Tolerance mechanisms are needed for the adaptive system, whose randomly generated receptors can statistically bind self.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28-B7 costimulation is a requirement for priming naive T cells, not a gate on innate macrophage activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow B-cell mechanism that replaces a self-reactive light chain; innate cells do not edit their receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymic deletion (negative selection) screens randomly generated T-cell receptors on developing lymphocytes; innate PRRs are germline-encoded and are not screened in the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-2 consumption by CD25 on Tregs deprives other T cells of a growth signal; it is not how innate cells are kept from responding to self.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A mature naive CD4+ T cell that left the thymus with a weakly self-reactive receptor later encounters its self-antigen in the spleen and is rendered non-responsive. Based on the location of this event and the cell population it acts on, it is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central tolerance, because the receptor was formed by V(D)J rearrangement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Central tolerance, because the spleen is a primary lymphoid organ

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune privilege, because the spleen tolerates introduced foreign antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance, acting on a mature lymphocyte in a secondary lymphoid organ

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive selection, because the cell survived contact with self-antigen

explanation.summary: Tolerance imposed on mature lymphocytes outside the thymus and bone marrow is peripheral tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines central tolerance as tolerance within the primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) acting on developing lymphocytes, and peripheral tolerance as tolerance anywhere else, including secondary lymphoid organs, the bloodstream, or tissues, acting on mature lymphocytes. A mature T cell silenced in the spleen fits the peripheral definition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All T-cell receptors are made by V(D)J rearrangement; what classifies tolerance as central versus peripheral is where it occurs and whether the lymphocyte is developing or mature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ; the primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune privilege refers to specific sites such as the eye, brain, and placenta that tolerate introduced antigens; the spleen is not described as a privileged site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Positive selection is a thymic-cortex event in which double-positive thymocytes that bind MHC weakly progress; it does not describe silencing of a mature peripheral T cell.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A thymocyte in the thymic cortex that expresses both CD4 and CD8 binds a self-peptide presented on MHC by a thymic epithelial cell with weak affinity. Which of the following is the most likely immediate result of this interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anergy resulting from the absence of a costimulatory signal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diversion into the regulatory T-cell lineage in the thymic cortex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative selection and elimination of the cell by apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive selection and progression to a single-positive cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing of its rearranged T-cell receptor genes

explanation.summary: Weak binding to peptide-MHC on thymic epithelium in the cortex is the signal for positive selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick recalls that in the thymic cortex, double-positive (CD4+/CD8+) T cells undergo positive selection and become single-positive cells when they weakly bind to peptides presented on MHC by thymic epithelial cells. Only after this do single-positive cells move on to negative selection in the medulla.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is a peripheral tolerance mechanism affecting mature T cells that see antigen without CD28-B7; it is not a thymic selection outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Treg diversion applies to CD4+ single-positive cells that bind at an intermediate level in the medulla, not to weakly binding double-positive cells in the cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection occurs in the thymic medulla and eliminates single-positive cells that bind self-peptide-MHC too strongly, not cortical cells that bind weakly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow B-cell process; T cells do not edit their receptors.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In the thymic medulla, a single-positive CD4+ thymocyte binds a self-peptide-MHC class II complex with an affinity that is too strong for release as a conventional naive T cell but not strong enough to trigger deletion. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion to an induced Treg by retinoic acid and TGF-beta

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion by Fas-FasL-mediated apoptosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diversion to become a CD25+ FoxP3+ regulatory T cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Export to the periphery as a conventional naive CD4+ T cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing at a light-chain locus

explanation.summary: Intermediate-affinity binding to self-peptide-MHC in the thymus diverts CD4+ thymocytes into the Treg lineage.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes generation of regulatory T cells as the secondary mechanism of T-cell central tolerance: a portion of CD4+ T cells that bind at an intermediate level may be diverted from their path to develop into Tregs, which express CD3, CD4, CD25, and the transcription factor FoxP3. Figure 1 shows strong binding leading to apoptosis, weak binding to circulation, and intermediate binding to the Treg cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retinoic acid and TGF-beta from tolerogenic dendritic cells generate induced Tregs in the periphery (gut), not in the thymic medulla.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fas-mediated deletion is the peripheral apoptosis pathway; thymic deletion requires strong binding, which this cell does not show.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only thymocytes that bind MHC-peptide weakly are allowed to exit to the periphery as conventional naive T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing occurs in developing B cells in the bone marrow, not in thymocytes.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A researcher wants to isolate thymus-derived regulatory T cells from peripheral blood by flow cytometry. Which of the following marker combinations best identifies this population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3, CD4, B7, and CTLA-4

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD3, CD4, CD25, and FoxP3

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD3, CD4, CD40L, and PD-L1

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD3, CD8, CD28, and Fas

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD19, IgM, CD40, and FcgammaRIIB

explanation.summary: Tregs are CD3+ CD4+ CD25+ FoxP3+ T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that Tregs are characterized by their expression of CD3 (like all T cells), CD4, CD25 (the high-affinity IL-2 receptor), and the transcription factor FoxP3. This combination distinguishes them from conventional CD4+ helper cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 (CD80/CD86) is expressed on antigen-presenting cells, not on Tregs; although Tregs do express CTLA-4, this set lacks the defining CD25 and FoxP3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD40L is the helper T-cell ligand that provides CD40 help to B cells, and PD-L1 is a ligand on tumors and privileged tissues; neither defines Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tregs are CD4+, not CD8+; CD8 with CD28 and Fas describes a conventional cytotoxic T cell, not a regulatory cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD19, IgM, CD40, and FcgammaRIIB are B-cell markers, not T-cell markers.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: After positive selection, negative selection, and diversion of some cells into the regulatory T-cell lineage, approximately what proportion of developing thymocytes is ultimately released into the circulation as mature naive CD4+ or CD8+ T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50%

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 90%

explanation.summary: Only about 5% to 10% of thymocytes survive thymic selection and exit as mature naive T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that after positive selection, negative selection, and generation of Tregs, only 5% to 10% of developing thymocytes are eventually released into the circulation as mature naive CD4+ or CD8+ T cells. Only those that bind MHC-peptide complexes weakly are allowed to exit to the periphery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stated yield is 5% to 10%, well above 1%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A quarter or more of thymocytes surviving overstates the yield; most cells fail positive selection or are deleted.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Half of thymocytes surviving would imply far less stringent selection than the brick describes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vast majority of thymocytes are eliminated during selection; more than 90% is the proportion lost, not released.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy with IPEX syndrome confirmed by a FOXP3 loss-of-function mutation is receiving corticosteroids and a T-cell inhibitor, with only partial control of his enteropathy and autoimmune endocrinopathy. Which of the following interventions has the potential to restore a functional regulatory T-cell population rather than only suppressing his autoreactive effector cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addition of a second T-cell inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bone marrow transplantation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Escalation of corticosteroid dosing

explanation.summary: Bone marrow transplant can supply FOXP3-competent progenitors and thus functional Tregs in IPEX.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that IPEX patients, who lack Tregs because of FOXP3 loss-of-function mutations, are treated with immunosuppressive therapies including steroids and T-cell inhibitors, and are sometimes given a bone marrow transplant. Because Tregs are generated from developing lymphocytes, replacing the hematopoietic source through transplantation is the intervention that can restore the missing Treg population; the drugs only suppress effector cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T-cell inhibitors suppress effector T-cell activity but do not correct the underlying inability to make functional Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking CTLA-4 removes a brake on T-cell activation and would worsen, not improve, autoimmunity in a patient already lacking Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking PD-1 turns activation signals back on and is used to unleash anti-tumor responses; it would aggravate autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids are part of the immunosuppressive regimen that dampens autoreactive effector cells; they cannot generate FOXP3-expressing Tregs.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In the bone marrow, an immature B cell whose IgM receptor binds a soluble self-antigen initiates a new round of V-J recombination at its lambda light-chain locus. The resulting receptor, now paired with the original mu heavy chain, still binds the self-antigen with high affinity. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonal deletion by apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Export to a Peyer's patch for suppression by induced Tregs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive selection because a new receptor was generated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rearrangement of the mu heavy-chain locus to remove self-reactivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release into the circulation as an anergic B cell

explanation.summary: A B cell that still binds self-antigen after receptor editing is deleted by apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that receptor editing lets an immature B cell start another round of VJ recombination in its kappa or lambda light-chain loci to try to generate a receptor that does not bind self-antigen. If successful, the cell leaves the bone marrow (Figure 2, pathway B); BCRs that continue to bind self-antigens undergo apoptosis (Figure 2, pathway C). This cell's edited receptor still binds self, so it dies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Central tolerance is completed in the bone marrow; there is no described pathway exporting failed B cells to the gut for Treg suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Merely generating a new receptor is not enough; the edited cell is tested again for autoreactivity and only non-self-binding receptors allow the cell to leave the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor editing as described involves the kappa or lambda light-chain loci; the initial BCR's mu heavy chain is retained, not re-edited.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Self-reactive immature B cells that fail editing are deleted in the marrow, not exported; anergy is a peripheral mechanism for mature B cells lacking T-cell help.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a mechanism of central tolerance with the lymphocyte lineage and site in which it occurs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Generation of regulatory cells: B cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Negative selection: B cells only, not T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive selection: T cells only, not B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor editing: B cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing: T cells in the thymic medulla

explanation.summary: Only B cells edit their receptors (bone marrow) and only T cells become Tregs (thymus); both lineages undergo positive and negative selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, like T cells, B cells undergo positive and negative selection, but unlike T cells, B-cell central tolerance occurs in the bone marrow and includes receptor editing. It also emphasizes that only T cells can become regulatory cells (Tregs) and only B cells can go through receptor editing, the process of changing antigen receptors by switching the light chain expressed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Generation of regulatory cells during central tolerance is a T-cell (thymic) event; B cells do not become Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both T cells and B cells undergo negative selection of high-affinity self-binders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both T cells and B cells undergo positive selection according to the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T cells do not perform receptor editing; the thymic medulla is the site of negative selection and Treg generation.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In the absence of infection, a resting dendritic cell in a lymph node presents a peptide derived from normal tissue turnover on MHC class I to a naive CD8+ T cell whose TCR recognizes it, and the CD8 co-receptor engages. The T cell becomes unresponsive rather than proliferating. Which of the following best explains why the T cell was not primed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B7 (CD80/CD86) is upregulated only on inflammation-activated antigen-presenting cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Naive CD8+ T cells cannot signal through their co-receptor without CD4 help

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naive T cells require IL-10 and TGF-beta from dendritic cells to proliferate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resting dendritic cells do not express MHC class I molecules on their surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resting dendritic cells express FasL and induce apoptosis of naive T cells

explanation.summary: Costimulatory B7 appears only on activated APCs, so T cells seeing self-antigen in a non-inflammatory setting become anergic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that priming requires TCR binding to peptide-MHC, a co-receptor signal from CD4 or CD8, and costimulation via CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86). Because B7 is upregulated on activated antigen-presenting cells, T cells are primed only in an inflammatory environment; a resting dendritic cell presenting a self-peptide without infection lacks B7, so the recognizing T cell becomes anergic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The CD8 co-receptor signal was delivered; CD8+ T cells use CD8, not CD4, as their co-receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 and TGF-beta are anti-inflammatory cytokines that attenuate responses; they are not required growth signals for naive T-cell priming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem states the peptide was presented on MHC class I and recognized by the TCR; MHC expression is not the missing element.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FasL expression is confined to activated CD8+ CTLs, NK cells, and cells in immune-privileged sites, not resting dendritic cells; the outcome here is unresponsiveness, not death.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Regulatory T cells suppress other immune cells through four major mechanisms. Which of the following directly results in the death of an autoreactive effector T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumption of IL-2 through CD25

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delivery of perforin and granzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of CTLA-4 that blocks B7-CD28 binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of dendritic cell stimulation of T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of IL-10 and TGF-beta

explanation.summary: Of the Treg mechanisms, only perforin and granzyme delivery directly kills the autoreactive T cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists four Treg suppressive mechanisms: expression of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor (CD25), secretion of IL-10 and TGF-beta, expression of CTLA-4, and killing of autoreactive T cells through perforin and granzymes. Only the last produces an apoptotic target cell (Figure 4); the others block activation or starve the cell of growth signals without directly killing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Soaking up IL-2 inhibits proliferation and survival signaling of other T cells; it is deprivation rather than direct killing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 and blocks activation of effector CD4+ T cells, but it does not kill them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting dendritic cell stimulation prevents T-cell activation but does not directly destroy the autoreactive T cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-10 and TGF-beta attenuate the immune response and can shift effector cells toward a Treg phenotype, but they do not directly cause cell death.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: PD-L1 and PD-L2 engage PD-1 on T cells to switch off the activation signal even after CD28-B7 interaction has occurred. Apart from tumors, expression of these ligands is especially important at which of the following sites, where an immune response in any form is dangerous?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peyer's patches

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymic medulla

explanation.summary: PD-L1/PD-L2 protect tissues such as the brain where any immune response would be harmful.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PD-L1/2 are expressed in many contexts, but two important scenarios are on tumors (as a way to escape death) and at sites of the body where an immune response in any form is dangerous, giving the brain as the example. The brain is also listed among the sites of immune privilege along with the eye and placenta.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow is a primary lymphoid organ where B-cell central tolerance occurs; it is not the example of a PD-L1-protected site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peyer's patches are the functional unit of gut secondary lymphoid tissue, where tolerogenic dendritic cells act; they are not the site cited for PD-L1 protection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where immune responses are normally generated, not a site where any response is dangerous.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymic medulla removes self-reactive thymocytes by negative selection; PD-1 ligands are described in the context of peripheral tolerance, not thymic selection.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Regulatory T cells maintain peripheral tolerance by inhibiting dendritic cell stimulation of T-cell activation and by suppressing B-cell activation. Which of the following additional cell types has its proliferation inhibited by regulatory T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Goblet cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: M cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural killer cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paneth cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymic epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Tregs also restrain the innate arm by inhibiting natural killer cell proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that Tregs play an important role in maintaining peripheral tolerance by inhibiting dendritic cell stimulation of T-cell activation, suppressing B-cell activation, and inhibiting proliferation of natural killer cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Goblet cells are gut epithelial cells that secrete mucus to trap pathogens; the brick does not describe Treg control of their proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M cells are specialized epithelial cells that transport antigen to Peyer's patches; they are not immune cells regulated by Tregs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paneth cells release defensins in the gut; they are not described as targets of Treg suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymic epithelial cells present self-peptide-MHC to developing thymocytes; Tregs act in the periphery, not on thymic stroma.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In a co-culture experiment, effector T cells are stimulated with antigen and antigen-presenting cells in the lower chamber of a transwell plate, while regulatory T cells are placed in the upper chamber, separated by a membrane that allows only soluble molecules to pass. Excess exogenous IL-2 is added to the lower chamber. Effector T-cell proliferation is still significantly reduced compared with cultures lacking regulatory T cells. Which of the following Treg mechanisms best accounts for this suppression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumption of IL-2 through high-affinity CD25

choices.label: B
choices.text: CTLA-4 competition with CD28 for B7

choices.label: C
choices.text: Engagement of Fas on the effector cells by FasL

choices.label: D
choices.text: Killing through perforin and granzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of IL-10 and TGF-beta

explanation.summary: Contact-independent suppression that persists despite abundant IL-2 points to secreted IL-10 and TGF-beta.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) as a Treg mechanism; these cytokines attenuate the immune response. Because the membrane permits only soluble factors and IL-2 is supplied in excess, the remaining suppression must come from secreted cytokines crossing the membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD25 soaks up available IL-2 to deprive other T cells, but excess exogenous IL-2 was added, so IL-2 deprivation cannot explain the suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CTLA-4 competing with CD28 for B7 requires Treg contact with the antigen-presenting cell, which the membrane prevents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FasL is expressed by activated CD8+ CTLs, NK cells, and cells in immune-privileged sites; Fas-FasL killing is contact dependent and is not one of the four Treg mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perforin and granzyme delivery requires direct contact with the target cell and would produce dead cells rather than merely reduced proliferation across a membrane.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A self-reactive CD4+ T cell circulating in the periphery has upregulated Fas on its surface. Contact with which of the following cells is most likely to trigger its apoptosis through Fas signaling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A naive CD4+ helper T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thymic cortical epithelial cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: An activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: An immature B cell in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: An intestinal M cell

explanation.summary: FasL is restricted to activated CTLs, NK cells, and immune-privileged tissues, so these are the cells that can delete Fas-bearing lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that Fas is a receptor found on many cells, including T cells, whereas Fas ligand (FasL) expression is confined to the surface of activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (CTLs), natural killer cells, and cells within immune-privileged sites. When Fas binds FasL, the Fas-containing lymphocyte undergoes apoptosis, and Fas expression on self-reactive T cells is thought to be upregulated (Figure 5).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naive CD4+ helper T cells are not listed as FasL-expressing cells; FasL is confined to activated CTLs, NK cells, and privileged-site cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thymic cortical epithelial cells mediate positive selection of thymocytes and are not described as FasL-expressing killers of peripheral T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immature B cells in the marrow are themselves undergoing central tolerance; they do not express FasL to delete peripheral T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M cells transport antigen across the gut epithelium into Peyer's patches; they are not FasL-expressing effector cells.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome due to a defect in Fas-induced apoptosis has chronic splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. In addition to autoimmune cytopenias, he is at increased long-term risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaphylaxis to food antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of oral tolerance to dietary proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Malignancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyendocrinopathy with enteropathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rejection of a corneal transplant

explanation.summary: ALPS patients accumulate lymphocytes and are susceptible to malignancies as well as autoimmune cytopenias.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that individuals with defects in Fas-induced apoptosis accumulate circulating autoreactive T cells (ALPS), presenting in early childhood with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy from lymphocyte buildup, and that patients are susceptible to malignancies and autoimmune cytopenias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Food anaphylaxis reflects a Th2/IgE-dominated response to a dietary antigen, not a Fas apoptosis defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oral tolerance depends on tolerogenic gut dendritic cells and induced Tregs; ALPS is not described as impairing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyendocrinopathy with enteropathy is the IPEX phenotype caused by FOXP3 mutation and loss of Tregs, not by a Fas defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corneal grafts survive because the eye is an immune-privileged site; ALPS does not abolish immune privilege.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A mature B cell in the spleen binds a T-independent self-antigen and receives a strong signal through its B-cell receptor. No helper T cells specific for this antigen exist because they were deleted in the thymus. Which of the following is the most likely outcome for this B cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation and antibody secretion without T-cell help

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anergy because CD40 is not engaged by CD40L

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apoptosis triggered by IgG binding to FcgammaRIIB

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deletion by the perforin and granzymes of regulatory T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing to replace its light chain

explanation.summary: T-independent self-antigens can bypass the requirement for T-cell help and activate self-reactive B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick recalls that B cells do not need T-cell help to respond to T-independent antigens, and that if B cells recognize and receive strong signals from T-independent self-antigens in the periphery, they may become activated. The anergy safeguard based on missing CD40 help applies only to T-dependent antigens, so this cell escapes tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anergy from absent CD40L-CD40 help applies to T-dependent self-antigens; a strong T-independent signal does not require the second signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcgammaRIIB inhibition requires high IgG levels engaging the receptor; nothing in the scenario indicates that condition, and the strong T-independent signal drives activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perforin and granzyme killing by Tregs is described as targeting autoreactive T cells; it is not the outcome here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a central tolerance mechanism for immature B cells in the bone marrow, not for mature B cells in the spleen.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In T-cell priming, the second signal is delivered by CD28 on the T cell binding B7 on the antigen-presenting cell. For a B cell responding to a T-dependent antigen, which of the following interactions provides the analogous second signal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B7 on the B cell binding CD28 on the helper T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD40L on the helper T cell binding CD40 on the B cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: FasL on the helper T cell binding Fas on the B cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG immune complexes binding FcgammaRIIB on the B cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: PD-L1 on the B cell binding PD-1 on the helper T cell

explanation.summary: CD40L-CD40 is the B-cell costimulatory second signal, paralleling CD28-B7 in T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, like T cells, B cells require a costimulatory signal to undergo activation, and that B cells need a second signal, CD40, to respond to T-dependent antigens. The summary specifies that B-cell anergy involves lack of binding of CD40L (on T cells) to CD40 (on B cells) in addition to TCR and peptide-MHC class II and the CD4 co-receptor signal, and Figure 5 shows CD4+ helper T-cell CD40L engaging B-cell CD40 as signal 2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28-B7 is the T-cell costimulatory pair; the B-cell second signal comes through CD40, not through B7 on the B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FasL-Fas engagement triggers apoptosis of the Fas-bearing cell; it is a deletion mechanism, not costimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG binding FcgammaRIIB downregulates antibody production and promotes apoptosis; it is an inhibitory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L1 engaging PD-1 turns off T-cell activation; it is an inhibitory checkpoint, not a costimulatory signal.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Which of the following cells of the intestinal epithelium releases defensins, antimicrobial peptides that help limit the bacteria reaching the enterocyte layer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Goblet cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: M cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paneth cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resident IgA-secreting B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tolerogenic dendritic cells

explanation.summary: Paneth cells secrete defensins as part of the gut's antimicrobial barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the gut immune system: goblet cells secrete mucus to trap pathogens, Paneth cells release defensins (antimicrobial peptides), and resident B cells secrete IgA into the lumen to neutralize pathogens. All of these features limit the bacteria that pass the enterocyte layer, reduce inflammation, and prevent immune responses to food and the microbiome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps pathogens; they do not release defensins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M cells sample and transport antigens across the epithelium to Peyer's patches rather than secreting antimicrobial peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resident B cells secrete IgA into the lumen to neutralize pathogens, not defensins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerogenic dendritic cells secrete retinoic acid and TGF-beta to generate induced Tregs; they are not defensin-producing epithelial cells.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Specialized epithelial cells of the small intestine transport luminal antigens across their cell bodies and deposit them into an underlying structure described as the functional unit of the secondary lymphoid tissue of the gut. Which of the following correctly identifies these cells and that structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterocytes; bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Goblet cells; Peyer's patches

choices.label: C
choices.text: M cells; mesenteric lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: M cells; Peyer's patches

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paneth cells; lamina propria

explanation.summary: M cells shuttle antigen from the lumen into Peyer's patches, the gut's secondary lymphoid unit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that antigens are sampled by specialized epithelial cells called M cells, which transport antigens across their cell bodies and deposit them in Peyer's patches, the functional unit of the secondary lymphoid tissue of the gut. There, in the absence of infection, tolerogenic dendritic cells promote Treg differentiation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterocytes form the epithelial layer but are not the specialized antigen-sampling cells, and the bone marrow is a primary lymphoid organ.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Goblet cells secrete mucus; they are not the antigen-transporting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M cells deposit antigen directly into Peyer's patches; draining lymph nodes are where activated dendritic cells travel after infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paneth cells release defensins and do not transport antigen; the lamina propria is not the described lymphoid unit.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: Mice are fed large amounts of a foreign protein daily for several weeks. They are then immunized by injection with the same protein. Compared with mice that were never fed the protein, the fed mice fail to mount an immune response to the injection. This finding is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central tolerance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune privilege

choices.label: C
choices.text: Innate immune activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral tolerance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing

explanation.summary: Prior oral exposure suppressing the response to later injection of the same antigen is the classic definition of oral tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that oral tolerance is sometimes defined as an inhibition of immune responses to subsequent injections of proteins following oral exposure: if you feed a mouse lots of a foreign antigen over time and then try to immunize the mouse with that antigen, it will not develop an immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central tolerance acts on developing lymphocytes in the thymus and bone marrow against self-antigens, not on a fed foreign protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune privilege refers to sites such as the eye, brain, and placenta that tolerate introduced antigens; it is not a systemic effect of feeding antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The finding is a lack of response, and the innate system activates only in response to pathogen- or damage-associated patterns, not harmless food proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow B-cell mechanism that swaps light chains; it does not describe systemic unresponsiveness after oral exposure.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: In an animal model of multiple sclerosis, mice that already harbor myelin-reactive effector CD4+ T cells are fed myelin protein over several weeks, and disease activity is suppressed. Which of the following best explains how oral administration of a self-antigen can suppress an established effector response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fed antigen induces receptor editing in myelin-reactive B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fed antigen reaches the thymus and negatively selects myelin-reactive thymocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: M cells degrade the antigen so it is never presented to lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral antigen upregulates B7 on Peyer's patch dendritic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tolerogenic dendritic cells convert even already-primed T cells into induced Tregs

explanation.summary: Gut tolerogenic dendritic cells can re-program effector T cells into induced Tregs, suppressing ongoing autoimmunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that oral self-antigen administration has been shown to suppress autoimmune disease in animal models of multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes, and other autoimmune conditions. Mechanistically, in the absence of infection, specialized tolerogenic dendritic cells promote the differentiation of T cells, even effector T cells, to Tregs through secretion of retinoic acid and TGF-beta; these peripherally generated cells are induced Tregs (iTregs). This explains suppression of an already established effector population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor editing occurs in immature B cells in the bone marrow, not in mature peripheral B cells, and the disease here is T-cell mediated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Negative selection is a central tolerance process acting on developing thymocytes; it cannot remove mature effector T cells already in the periphery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M cells transport antigen across their cell bodies into Peyer's patches for presentation; they do not destroy it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Upregulating B7 would enhance CD28 costimulation and T-cell priming, which is the opposite of the tolerogenic outcome observed.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: An invasive bacterial pathogen breaches the intestinal epithelium and causes tissue damage. Which of the following best describes where the resulting adaptive immune response is initiated and how effector lymphocytes reach the gut?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated dendritic cells prime lymphocytes in draining lymph nodes; effectors return by the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: M cells prime lymphocytes within the lumen; effectors migrate back across the epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paneth cells prime lymphocytes in the bone marrow; effectors are secreted with IgA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic epithelial cells prime lymphocytes in the thymus; effectors travel through the lymphatics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tolerogenic dendritic cells prime lymphocytes in Peyer's patches; effectors diffuse through the lamina propria

explanation.summary: Infection switches the gut from tolerance to a classic response: activated DCs prime lymphocytes in draining nodes, and effectors home back via the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that if infection does occur, the invasive pathogens themselves or the damage resulting from them activates a classic immune response: activated dendritic cells travel to draining lymph nodes and activate B and T cells, which travel back to the gut via the circulation (Figure 7 shows CD4+ effector T cells arriving from the circulation).

whyWrongByChoice.B: M cells transport antigen; they do not prime lymphocytes, and priming does not occur in the lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paneth cells release defensins; they do not prime lymphocytes, and the bone marrow is not where gut responses are initiated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus is the site of T-cell development and central tolerance, not of priming responses to gut infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerogenic dendritic cells act in the absence of infection to generate induced Tregs; pathogen-driven damage activates dendritic cells, which instead migrate to draining lymph nodes.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receives a corneal transplant from a donor who was not MHC-matched. Five years later, the graft remains clear and functional without systemic immunosuppression. Which of the following best explains this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corneal grafts are protected by oral tolerance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corneal tissue does not express any antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor B cells underwent receptor editing after transplant

choices.label: D
choices.text: The eye is an immune-privileged site

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recipient's thymus deleted donor-reactive T cells

explanation.summary: Long-term survival of unmatched corneal grafts is the classic example of immune privilege.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that certain tissues and locations have immune privilege, meaning they can tolerate the introduction of antigens, even foreign ones, without eliciting an inflammatory immune response; for example, the majority of transplanted corneas, even from someone who is not MHC-matched, survive long-term. The eye, brain, and placenta are listed as sites of immune privilege, maintained by limiting antigen access, anti-inflammatory cytokines, FasL expression, and Tregs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral tolerance concerns antigens entering the digestive system; it does not protect an ocular graft.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Privilege means foreign antigens can be introduced without eliciting a response; it does not require the tissue to be antigen-free.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow process in the recipient's own developing B cells and has nothing to do with graft survival.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Central tolerance in the thymus deletes thymocytes reactive to the recipient's own self-antigens during development; it does not delete T cells reactive to a later transplanted donor's antigens.

questions.topicName: Immunologic Tolerance

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy of Mediterranean descent has recurrent 1- to 3-day episodes of high fever with severe abdominal pain, an erysipelas-like rash on the lower leg, and painful swelling of a single ankle. Episodes resolve spontaneously, and between attacks he is well. Extensive testing shows neutrophilic inflammation but no autoantibodies, and the pattern is autosomal recessive. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against a joint self-antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of negative selection allowing autoreactive T cells to escape the thymus

choices.label: C
choices.text: MHC class II presentation of a self-peptide to helper T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Molecular mimicry following a streptococcal infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyrin loss-of-function leading to unchecked inflammasome activity

explanation.summary: Familial Mediterranean fever is a monogenic autoinflammatory disease driven by dysregulated innate immunity, not autoantibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that pyrin is a suppressor of the inflammasome and that two autosomal recessive autoinflammatory diseases, familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) and mevalonate kinase deficiency, result from pyrin loss-of-function. This causes increased inflammasome activity and IL-1 overexpression. The described FMF symptoms (fever, peritonitis, erysipelas-like rash, and single-joint arthritis) match the brick exactly and reflect neutrophil/macrophage-driven inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibodies define autoimmune, not autoinflammatory, disease; FMF produces no self-reactive antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Escaped negative selection is a tolerance-failure mechanism of autoimmunity and does not explain an IL-1-driven autoinflammatory syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC class II presentation to helper T cells is an adaptive/autoimmune mechanism, whereas FMF is an innate autoinflammatory disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular mimicry underlies infection-triggered autoimmunity such as rheumatic fever, not a hereditary periodic fever syndrome.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with familial Mediterranean fever continues to have frequent febrile flares despite colchicine. Her physician starts canakinumab, and the attacks subside. Which of the following best describes how this drug works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds IL-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks the IL-6 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It depletes circulating B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits the complement protein C5

choices.label: E
choices.text: It neutralizes TNF-alpha

explanation.summary: Canakinumab is an anti-IL-1 monoclonal antibody used for IL-1-driven autoinflammatory disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explicitly names canakinumab as a monoclonal antibody that binds IL-1 and prevents it from binding to its receptor, and lists it as a possible treatment for both FMF and mevalonate kinase deficiency, which feature IL-1 overexpression from excess inflammasome activity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the IL-6 receptor describes a different agent; canakinumab acts on IL-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Canakinumab does not deplete B cells; it neutralizes a cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement C5 inhibition is unrelated to canakinumab's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is one of the three major pro-inflammatory cytokines, but canakinumab targets IL-1, not TNF-alpha.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has months of crampy abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhea, fatigue, and a 6-kg weight loss. Colonoscopy shows patchy transmural inflammation of the terminal ileum, and two of his relatives have a similar illness. Which of the following genetic changes is most strongly associated with his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A CTLA-4 allele that reduces its expression

choices.label: B
choices.text: A FOXP3 mutation abolishing regulatory T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: A NOD2 mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pyrin loss-of-function mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: HLA-B27 allele

explanation.summary: Crohn disease is an autoinflammatory IBD whose strongest risk factor is a NOD2 mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the strongest risk factor for Crohn disease is a mutation in NOD2, a pattern-recognition receptor that recognizes microbial components. Mutated NOD2 leads to inappropriate NF-kB activation in monocytes; carrying two mutated alleles raises risk 20- to 40-fold. The transmural ileal inflammation, weight loss, and diarrhea match the brick's description of Crohn disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CTLA-4 allele is an intrinsic risk factor cited for celiac disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and SLE, not the principal Crohn factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FOXP3 loss causes the monogenic autoimmune syndrome IPEX, not Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyrin mutations cause familial Mediterranean fever, not Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B27 is tied to spondyloarthropathies; although IBD-associated arthritis is B27-linked, the strongest Crohn risk factor is NOD2.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, and her symptoms and histology normalize on a strict gluten-free diet. Which HLA subtype is most strongly associated with her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HLA-DQ2/DQ8

choices.label: B
choices.text: HLA-DR2

choices.label: C
choices.text: HLA-DR4

choices.label: D
choices.text: HLA-B8

choices.label: E
choices.text: HLA-B27

explanation.summary: Celiac disease is associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to gluten peptides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 of the brick pairs HLA-DQ2/DQ8 with celiac disease. The brick adds that celiac disease is a type IV hypersensitivity directed against gluten and human epithelial proteins, that ~95% of patients express HLA-DQ2 with the rest carrying DQ8, and that risk is dose-dependent. Gluten-responsive villous atrophy is classic celiac disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DR2 is linked to multiple sclerosis, SLE, and Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and Addison disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-B8 is not among the HLA-disease associations emphasized in the brick for this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies, not celiac disease.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: Three weeks after an untreated sore throat, a 10-year-old boy develops migratory polyarthritis, a new heart murmur, subcutaneous nodules, and a serpiginous rash. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of his illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with cardiac proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells killing uninfected bystander cardiac cells during infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the myocardium by Streptococcus pyogenes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epitope spreading to nuclear self-antigens, as occurs in lupus

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with histamine release

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity reaction caused by molecular mimicry.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes acute rheumatic fever as a type 2 hypersensitivity reaction driven by antibodies generated through molecular mimicry: the patient makes antibodies against Streptococcus pyogenes M protein, and after the infection clears these antibodies bind cardiac proteins that resemble M protein. This produces the classic migratory polyarthritis, pancarditis, skin nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bystander activation involves CTLs during active infection, whereas rheumatic fever is antibody-mediated via mimicry after the infection clears.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatic carditis results from cross-reactive antibodies, not direct bacterial invasion of the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epitope spreading broadens an established autoimmune response and is highlighted for MS, SLE, T1DM, and pemphigus, not for the initiation of rheumatic fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity is not the mechanism; rheumatic fever is a type II antibody-mediated reaction.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman reports drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day, along with fatigable limb weakness. Serum testing detects antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor. Which of the following best classifies the mechanism of her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibody causing cellular dysfunction (type II hypersensitivity)

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell activation and histamine release (type I)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune-complex deposition in vessel walls (type III hypersensitivity)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammasome-driven IL-1 overexpression by innate immune cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity to a self-peptide (type IV)

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis is a type II hypersensitivity in which anti-AChR autoantibodies block receptor function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that autoantibody directed to the acetylcholine receptor (anti-AChR) induces myasthenia gravis, a type 2 hypersensitivity reaction characterized by cellular dysfunction. It also notes in the summary that antigen specificity determines effect, with the anti-AChR antibody blocking receptor function, matching the fatigable weakness described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I IgE-mediated allergy is unrelated to anti-AChR autoantibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type III immune-complex disease describes conditions like SLE and rheumatoid arthritis, not the receptor-blocking mechanism of myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-1-driven inflammasome activity is an autoinflammatory (innate) mechanism, whereas myasthenia gravis is an autoantibody-mediated autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated (e.g., celiac disease), not the antibody-mediated process here.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgias, and fatigue. Laboratory studies show a positive ANA with anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Sm antibodies, and renal biopsy reveals immune-complex deposition. This disease is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An autoinflammatory reaction of the innate immune system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type III

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV

explanation.summary: SLE is a type III hypersensitivity disease driven by autoantibodies to nuclear antigens forming immune complexes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies SLE as a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction causing systemic inflammation and notes that SLE patients may have anti-DNA, anti-Sm, anti-histone, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies directed at nuclear and organelle proteins. Immune-complex deposition (as in the renal biopsy) is the hallmark of type III reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SLE is an adaptive autoimmune disease with autoantibodies, not an innate autoinflammatory disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I is IgE-mediated allergy and does not describe immune-complex lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type II involves antibodies against a fixed cell or tissue antigen (e.g., anti-AChR in myasthenia gravis), not soluble immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV is T-cell mediated (e.g., celiac disease), whereas SLE is antibody/immune-complex driven.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A researcher studies why a patient's mature T cells attack a normal self-protein. She concludes the T cell should have been eliminated while still developing but was not. Which tolerance process most likely failed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affinity maturation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anergy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bystander activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complement activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negative selection

explanation.summary: Central tolerance uses negative selection in the thymus to delete developing self-reactive T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that central tolerance occurs in the thymus (T cells) and bone marrow (B cells) and consists of deleting self-reactive lymphocytes by negative selection, acting on developing lymphocytes. A self-reactive T cell that should have been removed during development escaped negative selection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Affinity maturation refines antibody binding and does not delete autoreactive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anergy is a peripheral tolerance mechanism acting on already-circulating mature lymphocytes, not developing ones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bystander activation is an infection-driven mechanism of breaking tolerance, not a developmental deletion step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement activation is an effector amplification loop, unrelated to lymphocyte development.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases

questions.stem: A student is asked how peripheral tolerance differs from central tolerance. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance can additionally induce tolerance to harmless foreign antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance generates MHC molecules for antigen presentation by dendritic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance is independent of regulatory T cells and their cytokines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance occurs only within the thymus during T cell development

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral tolerance relies solely on negative selection of developing lymphocytes

explanation.summary: Peripheral tolerance controls circulating lymphocytes and can extend to harmless foreign antigens, not just self.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that central tolerance induces tolerance against self-antigens, while peripheral tolerance can additionally induce tolerance against harmless foreign antigens, such as food. Peripheral tolerance acts on circulating lymphocytes through deletion, anergy, and inhibition by regulatory T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tolerance mechanisms do not generate MHC molecules; MHC is encoded by HLA genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regulatory T cells are central to peripheral tolerance, so it is not independent of them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus is the site of central tolerance; peripheral tolerance acts on circulating lymphocytes in the periphery.
